title: Goods for all
hook: private property is real, but the earth's goods are meant for everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday, trafficking, and Josephine Bakhita, whose name means fortunate. Your line was no one for sale. Did you save that hotline number? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

"The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." That's a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims. Now look around the room you're in. The chair is yours. The phone is yours. Maybe the walls are yours, or the bank's. Catholic teaching says those claims are real. You can own things, and nobody gets to just take them. But it also says that underneath every deed and receipt, there's an older claim, and it belongs to everyone. The Church has a long, slightly clunky name for it. Today is that name, and the two truths it holds together.
screen: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` → `THE CHAIR IS YOURS.` → `AN OLDER CLAIM UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: The name is the universal destination of goods. Destination here means purpose: where the goods of the earth are meant to go. First, the gift. The Catechism begins at the beginning: God entrusted the earth and its resources to the whole human race, to take care of them and enjoy their fruits. The land, the water, the harvest were a gift to everyone before they were anyone's. Second, property is real. The Church doesn't abolish ownership. The Catechism defends the right to private property: people need a measure of security, a home, the freedom to plan and provide for their families. Owning things, rightly used, is good. Third, the two hold together. The Catechism says the right to private property does not do away with the original gift of the earth to all. So what you own, you hold as a kind of steward. The Second Vatican Council puts it this way in Gaudium et Spes: a person should regard the things they lawfully possess as common in this sense, that they can benefit others as well as themselves. Fourth, the early Church. In the Acts of the Apostles, the believers in Jerusalem shared what they had, and the Douay-Rheims says that "all things were common unto them." Catholic teaching doesn't require everyone to live that way. Religious orders live something like it. But it stands as a picture of where the goods of the earth are headed. So in daily life, the question isn't, is this mine? It usually is. The question is, what is this for?
screen: `THE EARTH: A GIFT TO EVERYONE.` · `PRIVATE PROPERTY IS REAL.` · `YOU HOLD IT AS A STEWARD.` · `ALL THINGS WERE COMMON.` · then, large: `WHAT IS THIS FOR?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing you own to share. Settle, and breathe. Go through your home in your mind, slowly, room by room. Notice what's sitting unused: a coat in the closet, tools in the garage, books on a shelf, a spare room, a car that sits all day. Don't feel guilty about any of it. Just ask of each thing: what is this for? Then pick one you could lend or give, and one person or group who could use it. If you pray, you can thank God for what you have. If you don't, simply hold the thing you chose, and the person, together. The bell holds the time.
Universal destination of goods. Private property is real, but the earth's goods are meant, in the end, to serve everyone. Today's word.
Your line: meant for all. Today, lend or give away the one thing you chose, to someone who'll use it. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics live out the universal destination of goods through almsgiving, parish sharing programs and food banks, lending and giving what sits unused, and, in religious orders, holding property in common.

options: it's your car; keep it in the driveway.
give the car away for good.

fork.reveal: the teaching keeps ownership real, and asks what it's for: things lawfully owned can benefit others as well as yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Church is against owning things.
what it means: ownership is real and good, but the earth's goods are meant, in the end, to serve everyone, so you hold what you own as a steward.
